_doc: Every line an NPC says (sim_core::npcs::LinesFile), by roster id (students share `students`). Picked and shown on the talking player's screen only (LinesFile::pick: seeded, weighted among the lines whose conditions hold); no message carries a line. when: pass (portraits, walking past; at most 90 characters), talk (on interact), hint (portraits: a VAGUE hint toward `secret`, said only while the player has not found it; never a precise place), gift (with today's gift; `gift` narrows it to lore | item | house_point | hint), given (today's gift already given), shop (a shopkeeper's greeting as the shop opens). Conditions, each optional: house (same | other, relative to the NPC's house, or a list of house ids), period ([morning, afternoon, night]), cup (yours_leads | other_leads | tied), wears (a catalog tag the player wears), weight 1-10. Placeholders {name} {house}, and in gift lines of their kind {place} {item} {lore} {points}. At most 160 characters. Our own invented, in-world text; adults; never sexualised. LinesFile::check_counts is the content gate (portraits 20-30 lines). docs/architecture.md 'NPCs'.

portrait_gs_l1.text: Make way! A scholar ascends!
Hark, a fine figure on the stair!
Ta-ra! Onward and upward!
Announcing... oh, you've gone already.
Hark... quietly. Even heralds whisper after dark.
Presenting {name} of {house}, bold of heart and loud of boot! Ta-ra! Forgive me, I never could resist a fanfare.
Behold {name} of {house}, steadfast and true! The finest fanfare is the one you've earned, and you've earned several.
Announcing {name} of {house}, keen of mind! I'd list your accomplishments, but I suspect you'd correct the order.
Presenting {name} of {house}, who arrives exactly when intended! A herald does admire a dignified entrance.
Good morning! A herald's first duty is to announce the day. Day, you are announced. Splendid.
The afternoon procession! Half the castle climbs these stairs after lunch, and the other half comes down looking for it.
Late on the stairs, are we? I shall announce you very softly. Ta-ra. There. Most discreet.
These stairs began to wander one cold winter, after an architect tried to make them easier. Easier, yes. Predictable, never.
The poor architect of these stairs wrote apology after apology. I once tried to announce the last one. Far too short for a fanfare.
One flight in this castle has never moved an inch. I like to think it heard the charm coming and stood its ground. Admirable.
Your house leads the Cup! I've been practising a victory fanfare. It's mostly trumpets.
Your house trails in the Cup this week. Chin up! A good herald can make third place sound like a coronation.
The hourglasses are neck and neck! I've prepared a fanfare for every outcome, and one for a draw.
Dress robes! Now there's an outfit worth announcing. Stand still a moment while I find the right trumpet.
Velvet! A herald knows velvet. You look ready to be presented at court.
I announced a king once. Well, a man named King. He was a cooper, but he took it very graciously.
I've announced people coming down from floors they never walked up to. There's more than one way between the upper storeys.
I once announced a gentleman who swore he'd stepped clean through marble. I took him for a poet. Now I'm not so sure.

portrait_gs_l3.text: Shoulders back. Better.
Boots: passable. Carry on.
Seven out of ten for posture.
Punctual, I hope?
Walk, don't scurry.
{house}. Courage earns full marks; pausing at the top of the stairs before charging on earns more. Do try it.
{house}. Diligent, honest, reliable. I'd mark you higher if you stopped apologising to the banisters.
{house}. Your answers are usually right. Your handwriting, I suspect, is not. Neatness counts, {name}.
{house}. Ambition is a fine subject. Mind it doesn't crowd out the others; I examine all of them.
Good morning. You're up and dressed, which already puts you ahead of a third of the castle.
The afternoon is when attention wanders. I shall be watching for yawns. That was very nearly one.
It is late. I'd deduct marks for the hour, but I'm retired, and nobody will let me.
The old timetables rang a bell for every lesson. Eighteen in a day! I always thought the bell ringer had a point.
Every classroom once kept a spare chair for a late professor. Sit in one and you'll get the hardest question. I set a few myself.
The oldest inkwells refill themselves at midnight. I still say a student should mix her own ink. It builds character, and blue fingers.
Your house leads the Cup. Satisfactory. Now keep it there; leading is easy, staying is the examination.
Your house is behind this week. Not a failing grade. Merely a note in the margin: could do better.
A tie at the top. In my day we'd have settled it with a written paper. Three hours, no talking.
Correct school dress, neatly worn. You'd be surprised how rarely I can say that. Full marks.
Knitwear. Sensible on these stairs; the draught on this landing is a disgrace. Check your cuffs for loose threads.
I examined for forty years. The most common wrong answer? Panic. Never panic. Then think.
Polished things rarely hide anything, except when they do. If you're ever downstairs among the cups, examine closely.
The best scholars find the quickest route between their books and their lessons. Some routes appear on no timetable.

portrait_gs_l4.text: Mm. Looks like rain.
Shh, they're biting.
Mornin'... or is it?
Had a bite once. Lost it.
Mind the drips.
{house}, eh? Bold lot. You'd wade straight in after a pike. I'd wait for it to come to me. That's why I've still got all my toes.
{house}, is it? Patient folk. You'd make good anglers. Sit, wait, eat your sandwich. Mostly the sandwich.
{house}. You'll want to know how deep the lake is. Deeper than my line, that's how. Never found the bottom. Never wanted to.
{house}. You sleep down by the lake windows, don't you? Tell me, do the fish look in at you? Always wondered.
Best fishing's at first light. Mist on the water, kettle on the bank. Then the fish wake up and spoil it.
Afternoon's for dozing. Fish doze too. That's what I tell myself when nothing bites.
Night fishing? Can't see the float. Can't see the fish. Can't see the point. Off to bed with you.
Some autumn mornings the mist comes off the lake in the shape of this very castle. Saw it once. Nearly dropped my pike.
First frost, the lake goes silver for an hour. Lovely to look at. Nothing'll bite on a silver morning, mind.
My grandad said the shallows turned purple once a summer, when the castle dyed its robes by the lake. Fish came out lavender.
Your house is winning, they say. Don't let it go to your head. The big ones always get away at the last moment.
Behind in the Cup? Bah. Fishing's taught me one thing: sit tight, keep your line wet, and the tide turns.
All square at the top, I hear. Like two lads hooking the same fish. Someone's going in the lake.
Good thick cloak, that. You'd do for a day on the bank. Rain runs straight off. Wish I'd been painted in one.
Rolled sleeves? Proper fishing look, that. All you need is a worm and a great deal of patience.
This pike? Caught him myself. The one I wanted was twice the size. Got away. He's still out there, laughing at me.
Down where it's damp, there's a breeze that smells of old apples and barrels. Breezes come from somewhere, don't they?
Seen folk come down from the floor above without touching the stairs. Didn't ask. A good fisherman never asks where the fish came from.

portrait_gs_l5.text: Oh! Have you heard?
Psst. Later, darling.
Don't look now. Actually, do.
Scandal, darling. Simply scandal.
Out at this hour? How delicious.
A {house}! Your lot are always in the thick of something. Do come back and tell me what. Embellish freely; I always do.
A {house}! You're the ones who know everything and say nothing. Utterly maddening. Tell me one small thing. Anything.
A {house}! You lot read the old records. Is it true about the founding prefects? No, don't tell me. I prefer my version.
A {house}! You appreciate the value of a well-placed secret. We should trade, darling. I'll go first. Eventually.
Morning gossip is the freshest, darling. Things happened overnight. They always do.
The afternoon lull. Nobody has done anything scandalous since lunch. I'm reduced to inventing it.
Out at this hour? Darling, how delightfully suspicious. I shan't tell a soul. Well, one soul.
The prefects once signed a promise to keep every corridor lit, then hid the parchment so nobody could find it. Scandalous! I adore them.
The painter of half these portraits painted herself in forty different hats. Which one am I? A lady never says.
The losing houses used to sew pennants for the winners. The stitches grew smaller and nastier every year. Such delicious spite.
One spring the hall clock ran backwards for a week. Students claimed they'd handed in essays before writing them. I believed every word.
Your house leads the Cup! Everyone's talking about it. Well, I am. Which is the same thing.
Behind in the Cup, darling? I hear the leaders are getting smug. Smugness always comes before a fall. I'll save you a seat.
A tie at the top! The tension, darling. I haven't been this thrilled since the business with the moving stairs and the vicar.
That hair ornament! Who are you trying to impress? No, don't say. Let me guess for a week.
Darling, that outfit. Bold. Very bold. People will talk. I'll make sure of it.
Two hundred years on this wall and I've never spread a false rumour. Exaggerated, yes. Improved, often.
They say a lovesick sculptor walked through one of his own statues and came out somewhere far below. I say it's true. It's romantic.
Someone once vanished among the trophies and turned up for supper on time. Nobody has ever explained it. I have six theories.

portrait_gs_l6.text: Which way is north today?
Lost? Me too. Splendid!
Left! No, right. No...
Mind the stairs, they cheat.
Ahoy! Is this the sixth?
{house}! You charge up these stairs like they owe you money. They do, in a way. They've stolen hours from all of us.
{house}! Reliable people. If I'd had one of you on my expeditions, someone would have remembered to pack the map.
{house}! Splendid, you'll know which floor this is. I've had it as the sixth, the ninth and once, briefly, the cellar.
{house}! You lot live down under everything, don't you? I tried to map the dungeons once. I ended up in the kitchens.
Morning! The stairs are usually calm before breakfast. I say usually. I've been wrong about everything else.
Afternoon! A fine time to get lost. Plenty of daylight left to be found by.
The stairs move most at dusk, you know. By night they're positively playful. Hold the rail and trust nothing.
An architect charmed these stairs to be easier and they've been impossible ever since. I've drawn sixty maps of them. All wrong.
There's meant to be a whole wing nobody can find. It's on the plans. I've looked for it for a century. Found several cupboards.
The stairs refused to lead anywhere as unpredictable as the fortune-telling room, so a ladder was hired. I respect that ladder.
Your house leads the Cup, I'm told! By whose map? Never mind. Congratulations, whichever way you're facing.
Behind in the Cup? A good navigator knows you can be lost for weeks and still arrive first.
All the hourglasses level? Like a compass that points everywhere at once. Exciting, and not much use.
A proper travelling coat! Pockets for maps, I trust? Use them. Mine are full of compasses that disagree.
School robes, eh? Sensible. If you get lost, at least everyone will know where to send you back to.
My finest map shows the castle exactly as it is. Unfortunately, the castle moved. I keep it for sentimental reasons.
I once took a wrong turn and found a stair the moving ones know nothing about. Somewhere below me. Rather woolly, as I recall.
There's a quick way from the reading rooms to a classroom, so I'm told. Never found it. Then again, I've never found anything.

portrait_great_hall_n.text: Elbows off the tables, please.
Napkin, dear. Napkin.
Walk, don't sprint, in my hall.
I've got your tally right here.
Feast's not ready. Shoo.
{house} table, yes? Lively. Last feast one of yours knocked a whole trifle over with a victory wave. I still have it in the ledger.
{house}! Your table always finishes everything and thanks the kitchens. I told the cooks. They wept.
{house}. Your table argues about the puddings with footnotes. I'm not complaining. I'm noting.
{house}. The tidiest table in the hall, I'll give you that. Also the most careful with the salt. Suspiciously careful.
Breakfast is the most important meal. Says me. Porridge first, then toast, and no reading at the table.
Lunch cleared, supper not yet laid. The most peaceful hour in my hall. Don't spoil it.
The hall's closed for the night. The candles stay up there only to keep me company.
The four tables came from one oak, split four ways so nobody got the better wood. They still argue about it. I've heard every side.
The first Cup was a pewter tankard. They drank warm milk from it until someone tried to brew in it. I'd have docked points.
The hourglass sand came from four different shores, one chosen by each house. I can tell them apart by the sound. Truly.
Beneath this hall hang the kitchen bells. A plate stays empty too long and its bell rings. I thoroughly approve of that bell.
As of this morning your house leads the Cup. I keep the tallies in my head, so don't let me catch you slacking.
Your house is behind this week. Not by much. A few good lessons and some decent manners would close it.
Tied at the top. I've counted twice. Someone at the high table will have to carve that cake very carefully.
Dress robes in my hall! Finally, someone who understands what a feast is for. Mind the gravy.
A jumper at table. Practical. Do roll your sleeves up before the soup; wool and soup are old enemies.
The cellarmen used to bring the feast barrels up in no time at all. Not by any stair I know of.
Some trophies have a way of travelling. Ask anyone who polishes them where the draught comes from.

portrait_great_hall_s.text: A bow is never wasted.
En garde! Only joking.
Good form, there.
Mind your footwork.
Ah, a duellist's stride.
{house}. Bravery is a duellist's first virtue. The second is knowing when to bow out. Learn the second; you have the first.
{house}. You fight fair, always. Good. A clean duel lost is worth more than a grubby one won. I've lost a few. Cleanly.
{house}. You'll be studying your opponent's habits. Clever. Mine was pausing to admire my own form. Fatal, mostly.
{house}. Patient duellists, your lot. You wait for the opening. I respect it, though I prefer to make my own.
Good morning. A duellist warms up before breakfast: a stretch, a bow, a second bow. The second is the important one.
Afternoon is when the Club gets busy. Do go along. And bow, for my sake. I can always tell from here.
Late, isn't it? My last great match ran past midnight. Neither of us would concede. We both fell asleep standing up.
Two friends founded the Dueling Club to settle their arguments formally. The arguments never ended, but heavens, they bowed beautifully.
The bow after a duel is deeper than the bow before. The winner owes a lesson; the loser owes a better duel. Remember that.
In my day we duelled on this very floor. I won forty-one matches and lost forty-two. Do ask me about each one. I have time.
Your house leads the Cup! Win it graciously. A gracious winner is invited back; a gloating one is hexed.
Behind in the Cup? A setback, not a defeat. I once came back from three points down with a sprained wrist and a cold.
A tie! The most honourable result there is. Both bow, nobody sulks. It never lasts, of course.
Dress robes! In my day we duelled in them. Ruined a great many cuffs. Worth every one.
Dragonhide boots! Grippy soles. You'll never slip mid-bow again. It took me thirty years to learn that.
Bow from the waist, not the neck. The neck is for nodding at acquaintances. An opponent deserves the whole spine.
My old rival once dodged behind some marble and simply wasn't there any more. Turned up downstairs for supper. Forfeited, technically.
My old trophies sit somewhere near this hall. The caretaker swears one of the cases has a draught. A draught! Behind a cup!

portrait_library_n.text: Shh.
Shhhh. Footsteps.
Whisper, please.
Ah, a reader. Shh.
Quietly, quietly.
{house}. You read the way you duel: all at once. Try one chapter. Then a footnote. Then breathe.
{house}. You return books on time. You have no idea how rare that is. I could weep. Quietly.
{house}! A kindred spirit. Have you read the appendix to the appendix? Nobody has. It's glorious.
{house}. You'll want the books that aren't on the shelves. They are on the shelves. Nobody looks properly.
Morning is the best time for reading. The ink is awake and the dust is still asleep.
The afternoon crowd. Pages turning like rain. Lovely. Until somebody sneezes.
The library at night. Every book holding its breath. Shouldn't you be in bed? Shouldn't I?
The rule above the door asks for whispers. It was carved by a librarian with a very loud voice. A note to herself, I believe. Footnote three.
The telescope lending book begins with a telescope that never came back. I've a few library books in much the same state.
The archive holds forty-one letters of apology about the stairs. I've annotated all of them. The last one needs no annotation at all.
Your house leads the Cup. Congratulations. Silently, please.
Behind in the Cup? Read more. Points follow knowledge as footnotes follow sentences.
A tie at the top. Both sides citing equal sources. Very scholarly. Very irritating.
A good jumper for the stacks. The draught by the far shelves is centuries old. I've written a paper on it.
Dress robes in the library? Bold. Mind the ink.
May I recommend A Treatise on Damp? Nine volumes. Nobody has opened it in two centuries. It's riveting.
Some books lead further than others. Some walls of books lead further still. That is all. Shh.
Some lessons are closer to these shelves than the stairs would have you believe. A footnote, merely.

portrait_library_s.text: Bless you, dear.
Mind the ladder, dear.
Catalogued you. Lovely.
Gently with the spines.
A {house}. Brave hearts make hasty readers. Take your time, dear; the castle's secrets keep, but library fines don't.
A {house}. You lot always help me reshelve. I keep a little card for each of you in my heart's own index.
A {house}. You'll want the old castle plans. Mind, dear, the castle doesn't always agree with them.
A {house}. The archive keeps quieter secrets than any common room. Patience opens them.
Good morning, dear. I've catalogued the dawn. It came in at a quarter past, as usual. A reliable sort.
Good afternoon. The library is at its busiest now, which means it's at its happiest. Books like being needed.
Out late, dear? I won't scold. Some of my best finds were made by candlelight, against the rules.
The plans show a wing the castle has forgotten. I've indexed it under 'missing'. Every few years someone finds the door. It's a cupboard.
The common room rugs hide three rows of pattern, one from each generation of weavers. I've found two. Don't tell me the third.
The first lamp warden named all four hundred lamps and noted which ones sulked. I have her list. One of them still sulks.
Your house leads the Cup, I see. I keep a record of every week's standings, centuries back. Yours will be a nice entry.
Behind this week, dear? My archive is full of houses that came back from further. Here's to being one of them.
A tie! I'll have to rule a new column. I do love a new column.
A warm jumper, good. Archives are cold. Old paper likes the cold; old archivists less so.
Proper school robes. The archive has paintings of students in nearly the same cut, four hundred years back. Some things are right first time.
My index has a curious entry: 'stair, woven, upper floors'. That's all it says. I didn't write it, dear, and the castle won't explain.
There's an old note in my files: 'the polishers' stair, behind the shine'. Whoever wrote it was fond of riddles.
An old reader's diary mentions a door made of paint and patience, somewhere only a reader would think to look. That's all she wrote, dear.
One record speaks of marble that 'opens to the patient', somewhere among the castle's statues. Most records are less romantic.
The old cellar accounts list deliveries far quicker than the stairs allow. The cellarmen had their own way down, dear. A damp one, I imagine.

portrait_common_a.text: Halt! Oh. Carry on.
Who goes there? Ah, a friend!
Was that a shadow? Stand fast!
Forward! Er, after you.
Eek! Ahem. Good evening.
{house}! Comrade! Should any shadow trouble you in this corridor, call for me. I'll challenge it. From here. Loudly.
Ho, a {house} on the seventh floor! Loyal soul! Have you come to keep watch with me? I could use the company. For morale.
A {house}, so high up? Tell me, scholar, is there a word for a shadow that moves when you're not looking? I wish to challenge it by name.
A {house}, up here? I shall keep one eye on you and the other on that suit of armour. Both deeply suspicious.
Dawn! The shadows retreat! I'd like to think it's because of me. Let me think it.
The afternoon watch. Long, quiet, perilous. A fly landed on my helmet an hour ago. I bested it.
Night on the seventh floor. Every shadow a foe, every creak a charge. I've challenged that suit of armour nine times tonight.
Along this corridor your footsteps echo a moment late. I've stopped suddenly to catch it out. It stopped too. Fiend.
Portraits guard the common rooms because the keys kept vanishing. We judge the passwords, you know. I'm a harsh judge. Harsh but startled.
The hearths behind these walls have never gone out. Brave fires. They burn higher on cold nights. I like to think they're cheering me on.
Your house leads the Cup! Huzzah! I'd raise my sword, but the last time I did that I frightened myself.
Behind in the Cup? Then we charge! Figuratively. Through lessons, mostly. Charge through your lessons!
A tie! A standoff! Like two knights on a narrow bridge. Somebody has to blink. It's usually me.
A sturdy dark cloak. Excellent for night patrols, or for startling knights. Please don't.
A splendid hat! With a plume you'd pass for a herald. My friend on the first landing would be beside himself.
I was painted mid-charge. My horse was painted mid-bolt. We have never agreed on which direction we were going.
Somewhere below this floor a squire once stepped out of a wall-hanging. I challenged him from afar. He'd only taken a shortcut.
They say deep under the castle the walls breathe where the cellarmen once walked. I'm glad I'm up here.

portrait_common_b.text: Ey up, duck.
Had your tea, duck?
You look peaky. Eat something.
Mind the barrels, duck.
Kitchens are that way, love.
{house}, duck? All that charging about. You'll want a proper breakfast in you. Charge on a full stomach, I always say.
Hello duck, home again! Wipe your feet, warm your hands. There's always something hot going in the kitchens.
A {house} down here, duck? You've been reading through supper again, haven't you. I can tell. Go and eat.
A {house}, duck? You've come a long way from your chilly dungeon. Stop for a bite; nobody's watching.
Morning, duck! Porridge is on. Mind it doesn't stick. Mind you don't either; off to lessons after.
Afternoon, duck. Little something to keep you going till supper? Ask nicely in the kitchens; they'll find you a bun.
Up late, duck? Warm milk and bed, that's what you need. Not wandering about by the barrels.
These barrels? A cellarman stacked 'em here because he was sick of rolling 'em back. A house moved in behind and never left. Can't blame 'em.
The first cook here fed three hundred off a hearth meant for thirty, and there was always seconds. I'd have loved to brew for her.
There's an old iron pot in the kitchens nobody can lift. A spoonful of something goes in it every feast day. I know what. I'll never tell, duck.
Your lot's winning the Cup, duck! I knew it. It's all the good dinners.
Behind in the Cup, duck? Never mind. Eat up, sleep well, and you'll catch them. Works for barley, works for houses.
All tied up at the top, duck! Like a good brew: you wait, and wait, and then it's all ready at once.
Now that's a proper jumper, duck. Warm as toast. Did your gran knit it? Mine knitted this apron. Painted on, mind.
All neat in your school things, duck. Don't get gravy on 'em. Or do, and tell the laundry it was me.
I brewed a cordial once that made you hum for a week. Lovely tune. Nobody could stop. Not my best idea, duck.
My old cellarman came up from the deep cellars quicker than any stair allows. Said the walls down there had a draught. Funny man.
There's an old walk under the ground floor, all robes and stone. Folk turn up there from upstairs without using any stair I know.

portrait_common_c.text: What has eyes but sees no sky?
Are you coming or going?
Seen any stars today? No?
Why hurry, when stars don't?
Who walks past a riddle?
A {house} at the foot of my tower? Which is braver: to leap into the dark, or to wait for your eyes to adjust? Think on it.
A {house}! What grows stronger the more it's shared? Friendship? Bread? Both, I'd say. Have some of each.
Ah, {house}. What is always before you but never seen? The future, of course. And, today, your left bootlace.
A {house}? What's the cleverest move in a game nobody else knows you're playing? Answer that and I'll answer you.
Morning? What use is morning to an astronomer? It's when we sleep. So why are you awake? Why am I?
Afternoon. The stars are up there now, you know, merely hidden by the sun. Isn't that true of most things?
Night at last! How many stars can I count from this frame? None. How many can I imagine? All of them.
Do you know the old charts' constellations? The Lantern, the Heron, the Kettle. Why a Kettle? Why not, I ask you.
In one copy of the star charts the Heron wears a hat. Is that an error, or did the copyist see something we didn't?
Lightning took the tower roof three times, so they left it open. Isn't that the wisest answer to a question you can't stop being asked?
Your house leads the Cup. Is a lead a thing you hold, or a thing that holds you? Mind it doesn't.
Behind in the Cup? Does the moon mind being behind the sun? It catches up every month.
A tie. Two stars of equal brightness. Which do you wish on? Both, naturally.
Velvet, like the night sky. Did you choose it, or did it choose you? Clothes often do.
Knitwear. Why do astronomers always own jumpers? Because towers are cold and wonder doesn't pay for coal.
Why am I painted pointing at a star that isn't there? Perhaps it hasn't arrived yet. Perhaps I'm early.
What travels from page to wand faster than any stair? A shortcut, perhaps, between a quiet room and a lesson far below me?
What hangs on a wall, keeps out a draught, and lets a person through? Solve it on the floors below and you'll save your legs.

portrait_common_d.text: Oh. It's you.
I wasn't watching. I saw everything.
Do try not to drip.
Fascinating. Truly.
Mm. Your collar's crooked.
A {house}, down here. How thrilling. Do your boots always squeak this heroically, or is it an occasion?
A {house}. You're the only ones who ever ask how I am. Bored, darling. But thank you. It's... noted.
A {house}. Let me guess: you've come to study the damp. Fourteen kinds, at the last count. I counted. Out of boredom.
Ah, {house}. One of mine. Do come in out of the light; it does nobody any favours.
Morning. Such an energetic word. Down here it's mostly the same gloom with more yawning.
Afternoon. A procession to the Potions room, each student more nervous than the last. I give them marks. Silently.
Night. My favourite. Everyone creeps about thinking nobody's watching. Darling, I am always watching.
The Potions room was the castle's apple store once. On damp days you can still smell them. The only pleasant thing about the place.
The castle always has the last word, they say. Doors close a moment after you pass. I find that terribly well-mannered.
We portraits judge the passwords. I once turned away three prefects for poor pronunciation. One must keep standards.
Your house leads the Cup. How predictable. I mean that as the highest compliment.
Behind in the Cup? How very dull. Do something about it. Cleverly, if possible.
A tie. Everyone pretending not to care. Nobody cares more than when they pretend not to. I adore it.
Velvet. At last, someone with taste wanders past. I'd applaud, but I'm painted holding a glove.
Dress robes in a dungeon corridor. Either you're terribly lost or terribly stylish. I'll assume the second.
I was painted in three sittings. The painter talked through all of them. I've been silent ever since, out of protest. Mostly.
Somewhere down here a wall breathes. Cold air, old apples, older barrels. Not that I've noticed. I notice nothing.
Some robed stone upstairs is thinner than it looks. Don't ask how I know. I'm told things. I'm always told things.

portrait_kitchens.text: Something smells lovely, eh?
Peckish? Thought so.
Mind the flour, pet.
Don't touch the tarts!
Back for seconds?
A {house}! You eat like you mean it. I like that. There's a compliment for you. Now one for me?
{house}, pet! My best customers. The only ones who ever thank me for the crumble. I'd bake you a crown.
A {house}. You want the recipe, not the pie. Fine: two eggs, a lot of patience, and a pinch of not reading at the oven.
A {house}. Picky eaters, your lot, but you always come back for the treacle tart. Don't deny it. I've seen the crumbs.
Mornings, the ovens are hot and the bread's rising. So's the cook. Barely. Pass the tea.
Pastry for tonight's pudding. Cold hands, warm heart, that's the secret. Don't tell anyone.
Kitchens at night? You're after the leftover pie. I'm painted; I can't stop you. I can only tut.
Hear that bell? Some table upstairs has an empty plate. They ring all by themselves. Nobody knows who charmed them. Bless 'em.
The first cook here made a stew that fed the whole castle and still left seconds. I've tried for two hundred years. I get firsts.
Before there was a paddock, the creatures lived in the kitchens. One slept in a pudding basin on a feast morning. I made a new pudding.
Your house is top of the Cup, pet? I'll put an extra cherry on your table's trifle. Don't tell the others.
Behind, are you? Nothing a good pudding can't fix. Points are like pastry: let them rest, then roll on.
Tied at the top! I'll make two cakes. No, four. No... one big one, cut very fairly.
Lovely jumper. Keep it away from my oven; I lost a cardigan in there once. Toasted right through.
All dressed up in my kitchen! Mind the custard, pet. It goes for the good clothes first. No manners at all.
Pay me a compliment, pet, and I'll pay you a recipe. That's the kitchen's rate. Has been for centuries.
The cellarmen used to fetch the barrels faster than my bread could rise. Never took the stairs. Down where it's damp, they said.
A lad came down for cake once, smelling of polish, and said he'd come the quick way from among the cups. I gave him a bun anyway.

portrait_passage_weaver.text: Hm-hm-hmm... oh, hello.
Over, under, through.
Mind my threads, dearie.
Warp and weft, warp and weft.
Every thread goes somewhere.
A {house}. Bold threads, your lot. Always the first colour you notice in a pattern. Rarely the one holding it together.
A {house}! The threads nobody notices that hold the whole cloth together. Don't blush, dearie. It's the best thing to be.
A {house}. You'll see the pattern before I've finished weaving it. Spoils my surprise, dearie, every time.
A {house}. You like a pattern with a hidden figure in it, don't you? So do I. Look closer at most things.
Morning light's best for colour, dearie. I've been at the loom since before the owls. Hm-hm-hmm.
Afternoon. Halfway down a long row. Don't make me lose count. Forty-one, forty-two...
Night-weaving is all by feel, dearie. Like walking these corridors in the dark. You learn where the threads lead.
Three generations of weavers made the common room rugs, each slipping in a row nobody noticed. My cousins, dearie. Sneaky lot.
Madder for red, weld for yellow, woad for blue, all grown here once. The dye vats by the lake turned the shallows purple. Glorious.
One year the students knitted so many earmuffs for the gardeners that even the portraits got a pair. Mine's in a drawer.
Your house leads the Cup! A strong colour running right through the week's pattern. Keep it going, dearie.
Behind in the Cup? Patterns turn, dearie. Under, over, and then you're on top.
All the colours even at the top. A tartan of a week. I do like a tartan.
Oh, a knit! Let me see the stitch. Cable? Lovely. Somebody cared about that. Wear it in good health.
Good wool in that cloak, dearie. Hooded, too. You'll be warm on any stair in that.
Every thread goes somewhere, dearie. Follow one long enough and you'll end up where you never expected.
Not every hanging is only for looking at, dearie. Some keep a draught out. Some let a person through. Hm-hm-hmm.
There's a stair in this castle dressed in wool. Nearer than you'd think, and warmer than stone.
Pictures and weavings are cousins, dearie. One of my cousins keeps a stair for readers, so I'm told.

portrait_passage_trophy.text: Don't touch the glass!
Fingerprints! Everywhere!
Shiny, aren't they? I did that.
Mind the cups, please.
Dust. I can smell dust.
A {house}. Your house has more dented trophies than any other. Won hard, dropped harder. I polish out every dent personally.
A {house}! Your trophies are always the cleanest; you polish them yourselves. I've never been so moved, or so unemployed.
A {house}. Your cups are nearly all for written prizes. Very dignified. Very hard to dent. I approve.
A {house}. Your trophies stand at the front of every case. I don't know how. I put them at the back. Every morning.
Morning. First polish of the day. The light comes through just so, and every cup says good morning back.
Afternoon. Students on detention, polishing my cups. Badly. Up and down, not round and round! Honestly.
At night the cups gleam on their own in the moonlight. Then the dust comes out. I see it, you know. Every speck.
The stair next door was built to show our trophies to visitors. The visitors stopped coming. The trophies didn't. Now it's detention's job.
The first House Cup was a pewter tankard. Somebody tried to brew in it. I still have nightmares about the tarnish.
Tankard, bowl, goblet, hourglasses. The prefects like the hourglasses because nobody can drink from them. I say nobody can polish them properly.
Your house leads the Cup! I've already cleared a space in the case. Well, I cleared one for everybody. Just in case.
Behind in the Cup? Every trophy in here was won by somebody who was behind at some point. Except that one. Don't ask.
A tie! I'll need two polishing cloths. No, four. You never know.
Dragonhide boots. Lovely shine. May I? No? Just a quick buff? No? Fine.
That comb catches the light nicely. Have you considered a polish? Everything's better with a polish.
There's a cup in here for the longest hiccups. Twenty-one days. The winner never came to collect it. Couldn't stop.
Not every case in this room holds a cup, you know. I polish around one and it's always warm. Cases shouldn't be warm.
Dust settles everywhere in here except along one stretch of wall, where a little draught keeps it clean. I'd thank it, if I knew where it went.
Statues upstairs are never dusty. Suspicious, in my professional opinion. Something breathes behind marble.

portrait_passage_gallery.text: Stand still. Like that. Lovely.
You'd make a fine statue.
Marble's warmer than people.
Hush. The statues are thinking.
Ah... a profile!
A {house}. All motion and fire. You'd be impossible to sculpt. I'd have to carve you mid-leap and charge extra.
A {house}. A steady, kind face. I'd carve you in oak, not marble. Something that grows, something that keeps.
A {house}. You'd stand still for a portrait and think through all of it. I'd carve the thinking. The hardest part.
A {house}. Fine bones, a guarded look. You'd make an excellent bust. Busts never give anything away.
In the morning the gallery's light comes in low and the statues wake up. Not really. Nearly.
Afternoon light flattens everything. Even marble looks bored. Come back at dusk; it's worth it.
At night the statues are better company. They don't talk. Present company excepted, naturally.
Four robed figures stand in the niches here, and nobody knows who they are. Every year the students rename them. I call them my friends.
On midsummer morning the round window throws a perfect rose of light on this floor. Stand in it and forget your homework. Worth it.
The painter of my portrait painted herself forty times. I'd have carved myself once and stopped. Marble's dear.
Your house leads the Cup. I'd carve you a trophy, but they'd only put it with the others and dust it.
Behind in the Cup? Sculpture is mostly taking things away until what's left is right. Keep chipping.
A tie. Symmetry. Every sculptor's dream, and every House Cup's nightmare.
Velvet drapes beautifully. I spent a year carving folds like those and nobody noticed. You'd notice.
A hood and cloak. You'd stand in a niche and nobody would know you from marble. Don't, mind. The students would name you.
I prefer statues to people. No offence. Statues stay where you put them. Mostly.
Some of these marble folk are more door than stone, if you're patient with them. I won't say which. They're shy.
There's an old walk far below me, full of robed figures. Some of my statues miss it. They visit, I think, when nobody's looking.
Stone remembers. Somewhere far below, one stretch of wall remembers being a doorway for cellarmen.

portrait_entrance.text: Welcome in! Wipe your feet.
Mind the step, there.
Back again? Good to see you.
Doors are open, come in.
Ah, a {house}! I remember you. Came through those doors like a gust of wind on your first day. Still do.
A {house}! Welcome, welcome. You always say good morning to me. Not many do. It makes an old porter's day.
A {house}, nose in a book, never looking where you're going. Mind the step. There. You're welcome.
A {house}. Always know exactly where you're headed. I like that in a student. Saves me pointing.
Morning! The owls have been and gone. Post's on the tables, breakfast's in the hall, and the day's wide open.
Afternoon. Busy, busy. Half the castle in and out of these doors. I count every one. Habit.
Late, isn't it? The halls stay lit all night; the prefects promised that long ago. Off to bed with you, mind.
The Owl Exchange started with three quills traded for a pair of socks, one cold January. Best trade ever made, I reckon.
That clock once ran backwards for a whole week. Students swore they'd handed in essays before writing them. I had my doubts.
In the great snow they dug these very doors out from the inside. The students built a snow castle on the lawn. It fell over by teatime.
There used to be one notice board in here. So many notes it toppled one night like thunder. Next morning every common room had its own.
Your house is top of the Cup, I hear. Congratulations. I'll hold the doors a bit wider for you all week.
Behind in the Cup? Never mind. I've seen the hourglasses turn right round in a single week. Keep at it.
All square in the Cup! The whole hall's buzzing. Even the owls look excited, and owls never look anything.
Smart as paint in your school things. On your first day you had your robe on inside out. Don't worry, I never told.
Today's tip: tired legs between the upper floors? Not every stair is stone. Keep an eye on what's hanging about.
Today's tip: the shiny room off the ground floor is older than it looks. The polishers used to come and go without the door.
Today's tip: readers in a hurry once had a way up from their books that the moving stairs never knew about.
Today's tip: the castle's statues hold more than the pigeons' attention. One or two hold a way down, so they say.
Today's tip: the old cellarmen never rolled a barrel the long way round. Down where it's damp, there's a reason.

ghost_house_a.text: Ah, one of my own! {house} through and through. I can tell by the way you stand: ready to charge at something. Good.
{name}! Did I ever tell you I rode in the great tournament? I did. For about four seconds. Glorious seconds.
Hold your head up, {house}. I fell off a horse in front of three hundred people and I still have my pride. Somewhere.
A {house}, all the way up here? Bold of you. I like bold. Mind you don't tell anyone I said so.
You're not one of mine, but you've a rider's posture. Shoulders back, chin up. Now, never get on a horse.
Morning! In life I was up at dawn to groom my horse. In death I'm up at dawn out of habit. And spite.
Afternoon was the hour I rode out. Trumpets, banners, a crowd. Then a very short fall. Then a very long silence.
Night on the seventh floor. I drift up and down and practise my lance-work. Nobody's watching. Thank goodness.
There's a stretch up here where your footsteps echo a moment late. It isn't me. I don't have footsteps. I checked.
The fire in our common room has never once gone out. I warm my hands at it. Pointless, I know. It's the gesture.
If you duel, bow properly. I didn't bow before my joust. Some say that's why I fell. I say it was the horse.
The portraits judge our passwords, ever since the keys kept vanishing. Speak up clearly. They're sticklers.
On clear nights I float out to the balcony and look at the tower. Lightning took its roof three times. I admire anything that keeps getting up.
Your house leads the Cup! Well ridden. Stay in the saddle this time; it's the staying that counts.
Behind in the Cup? Pah. I've been behind on horseback. You know what you do? You hold on.
A tie at the top! Like two riders meeting in the middle of the lists. Somebody's ending up in the mud.
Our hourglass leads! I knew it. I'd cheer, but the last time I cheered I startled a student into a suit of armour.
Four seconds. That's how long my tournament lasted. Four magnificent seconds. I've been telling the story for four hundred years.
My horse was called Valiant. He wasn't. He stopped dead at the barrier and I didn't. That's the whole story.
People ask if it hurt. The fall, no. The laughter, a little. Four hundred years on, I've decided to laugh first.
A good cloak! A rider needs a cloak. Mine billowed beautifully, right up until I met the ground.
Dress robes! I wore my best to the tournament. You'd think falling off in them would have put me off. It hasn't.
I never leave this floor. The view's good, the company's brave, and the moving stairs make me seasick.
Shouldn't you be in bed, {house}? Go on. I'll keep watch. I'm very good at not sleeping.
Tell your house I said hello. And that I can still out-joust any of their ghosts. I've never tried. That's not the point.
Here's a tale for you, {house}: {lore}. I heard it from a ghost who heard it from a portrait. It's probably true.
Sit, listen. I'll tell you about {lore}. It isn't about me, for once. I know. I'm growing.
For good bearing and a brave heart: {points} to {house}. Don't spend it all at once.
I've a little sway with the hourglass. {points} for {house}. Ride well.
Every day one of mine rides past, I give them something. Today it's you. Here.
I've given you something already today. Come back tomorrow, and bring a better story than mine. Impossible, but try.
Already had your gift today, {name}. Greedy! I like it. Tomorrow.

ghost_house_b.text: Hello, petal! Home sweet home. Warm feet, full tummy, and a ghost who's always glad to see you. That's me. I'm the ghost.
{house}, my favourite! Don't tell the other houses. Actually, do. Wick-edly honest, I am. Sorry. Candle humour.
You look tired, love. Sit by the fire. It never goes out, you know. I'd be jealous, as a candlemaker, if I weren't so fond of it.
A {house} by the kitchens! Welcome, welcome. Nobody leaves down here hungry. Except me. I can't eat.
Not one of mine, but you've a kind face. Pop into the kitchens before you go. Say Hester sent you. They'll pretend not to hear.
Morning, petal! Smell that? Fresh bread. I can't eat it, but I can smell it, and that's half the joy. Well, a third.
Afternoon! The kitchens are rolling pastry for supper. I float through and supervise. Nobody asked me to. That's the fun.
Night already? I used to make the candles for nights like this. Now I'm too see-through to hold a match. Still, I glow a bit.
Why did the candle go to school? To get a little brighter. I've been saving that one for four hundred years.
I'm told I've a flickering personality. I take it as a compliment. Candles that don't flicker are no fun at all.
The barrels by our door were stacked there by a cellarman who got fed up. We moved in behind them. Best idea anyone ever had.
The kitchen bells ring when a plate's been empty too long. I try to ring one when I'm bored. Nobody notices. I'm a very quiet bell.
The first cook here, now there was a woman. Fed the whole castle from one pot. I made her candles. She said they smelled of honey. They did.
One year our lot knitted earmuffs for the gardeners and made far too many. The owls got some. A suit of armour got some. Mine fall through.
Your house leads the Cup! Lovely. I'll light a candle for you. A pretend one. It's the thought that counts.
Behind in the Cup? Never mind, petal. Slow and steady burns longest. Ask any candle.
All tied up at the top! Like a good wick. Something's about to catch.
Our hourglass is ahead! I knew it. All that hard work and kindness adds up, you know. It always does.
Oh, a lovely knit! Warm as a pantry. I was wearing a cardigan just like it when I took up haunting.
Nice and neat in your school things! Mind the gravy. I can't, you know. Goes straight through me.
Beeswax, that's what I smell of. Still. After all these years. I've decided it's my signature. Like perfume, but for ghosts.
I made the biggest candle the castle had ever seen. Then I sat down to admire it, and I've been admiring it ever since. In a manner of speaking.
Lost something? Ask me. I float through every drawer and cupboard down here. Hard to stop, once you start.
The kitchen corridor at teatime smells of toast and treacle. If I'm ever not here, check the kitchens. I'm in the kitchens.
Tell your house a ghost by the barrels says hello. And that she's very good company, and only a little bit chilly.
Here's a story to warm you, petal: {lore}. Better than a candle, and it'll never burn down.
Sit by me a minute. Let me tell you about {lore}. Someone told it to me, oh, a long time ago.
{points} for {house}! For being lovely. Don't argue; I've made up my mind, and I'm very stubborn for a candle.
There we are: {points} to {house}. Every little light adds up.
I always keep a little something back for our lot. Here, petal. With love from a waxy old ghost.
I've already given you something today, petal. Come back tomorrow. I'll still be here. I'm always here.
No more today, love, or the others will think I have favourites. I do. But they mustn't think it.

ghost_house_c.text: Ah. One of ours. Have you seen a comet? Small, green, a little shy. It's been missing for three hundred years. No? Well. Keep looking.
{house}. You have the look of someone thinking about something else. Good. That's where the best ideas are kept.
Ask a good question today, {name}. Not a clever one. A good one. They're rarer, and they last longer.
A {house}, all the way up here? Welcome. Mind the draught; it comes from the stars. Or the window. Probably the window.
You're not one of ours, but you're looking up. That counts for a great deal, up here.
Morning already? I was counting something. I've lost count. It was probably stars. It's always stars.
Afternoon. The sky is still up there, behind all that blue. People forget. I don't. I can't. I've tried.
A clear night! If you see a small green comet, would you tell it I'm here? It'll know the name.
The old charts have a constellation called the Kettle. I drew a copy of it once and gave it a spout. They told me off.
One copy of the star charts gives the Sleeping Hound two tails. I didn't do it. I might have done it. It was a long night.
The telescope lending book begins with a telescope that was never returned. I'm not saying it was mine. I'm not saying it wasn't.
Lightning struck the tower roof three times before they left it open. I was there for the third. Very bright. Very loud. Very wet.
Moonflowers open only at night. I pressed one in a book once, between lessons. I've forgotten which book. Three hundred years of looking.
Your house leads the Cup. Like a bright star in a quiet sky. Enjoy it. Stars move, you know. Slowly.
Behind in the Cup? My comet was behind everything too. Then it wasn't. Then it was gone. Hm. Not a helpful story.
A tie. A conjunction! Two bodies sharing the same point in the sky. Very rare. Very temporary.
Our hourglass leads. I'd celebrate, but I've forgotten how. Is it a sort of jig? I'll float about a bit.
Velvet. Like the sky just after sunset, before the stars come out. You wear it well.
A fine hat. The brim's wide enough to keep the starlight out of your eyes. Not that you'd want that.
I've been searching for one comet for three centuries. People say I should give up. People said that to the comet, too.
I once named a star after my cat. The cat didn't care. The star didn't either. But I did.
If you're up the tower, look east after midnight. There's nothing there. That's where my comet was. It's a very nice nothing.
The top of the tower has the best view in the castle. I drift up at midday to watch the owls. They pretend not to see me.
Go to bed, {house}. The stars will be there tomorrow. I'll make sure. Well, I'll watch. Same thing, really.
Tell your house a ghost in the tower says the sky is lovely tonight. It's always lovely. Tell them anyway.
Here, a little knowledge kept for you: {lore}. I wrote it down somewhere. Then I remembered it instead. Better.
Let me tell you about {lore}. I've told it to the stars many times. They're poor listeners.
For a good question: {points} to {house}. You did ask one. I heard it. You may not have noticed.
{points} for {house}. A small light, but small lights make constellations.
I find one thing a day worth giving away. Today, it's this. Mind you don't lose it. I would.
I've given you something already today, I think. Yes. I remember. Remarkable. Come back tomorrow.
Tomorrow, {name}. One gift a day, like one sunrise. I didn't make the rule. The sky did.

ghost_house_d.text: One of mine. Good. Sit down, think three moves ahead, and then make the fourth. Nobody expects the fourth.
{house}. The quiet ones win more games than the loud ones. Remember that the next time someone is very loud at you.
Every piece on the board matters, {name}. Even the pawns. Especially the pawns. They become something, if they get far enough.
A {house} in the dungeons. A bold opening. Let's see whether you have a middle game.
You're not one of mine. That's all right. I play all comers. I've lost only twice, and both times on purpose.
Morning. Most people waste the first move of the day. Don't. Breakfast first, then strategy.
The afternoon is the middle game. Everyone is tired, careless, overconfident. Be none of those.
Night. A good time to think. A better time to sleep. I'd recommend the sleep, but I've never managed it.
The Potions room was once an apple store. On damp days you can still smell the apples. I find it helps me think. Most things do.
The duelling bows are deep for a reason: the winner owes a lesson, the loser a better game. Chess has the same rule. I refined it.
The castle always has the last word, they say. I've been trying to beat it at that for three hundred years. A patient opponent.
Our hearth has never gone out. Some call it magic. I say it has simply never been given a reason. Everything needs a reason.
Your house leads the Cup. Good. Now is the dangerous moment. Leaders get careless. Don't.
Behind in the Cup? Then your opponents will relax. Let them. That's when you move.
A tie at the top. A stalemate. Stalemates are only dull to people who can't see the next move.
Our hourglass leads. I'm not surprised. I am pleased. Those are different things, and I allow myself both.
Dress robes in the dungeons. Either a statement or a mistake. I'll decide which once I've seen your next move.
Velvet. Understated, expensive-looking. Excellent choice. It tells people nothing, which is the point.
I died in the middle of a game. My opponent is still considering his move. He's been gone longer than I have.
Praise is rare from me. So: well done. For what? Work it out. That's the second half of the praise.
Never play a move you can't explain afterwards. Explaining it beforehand is optional.
I keep a board in the common room. The pieces move on their own at night. Mine. I'm winning.
Down here the corridors are quiet enough to hear yourself plan. That's why we live here. That, and the view of the lake.
Off to bed, {house}. A rested mind sees the whole board. A tired one sees only the piece in front of it.
Tell your house a ghost in the dungeons sends his regards, and will play any of them. Few accept twice.
Knowledge is a piece you keep off the board until you need it. Here's one: {lore}. Use it wisely.
Listen carefully; I'll say it once: {lore}. A story, and perhaps an advantage.
{points} to {house}. Earned, not given. I don't give. I recognise.
A small advantage: {points} for {house}. Small advantages win long games.
I reward cleverness. Today, you qualify. Don't make me regret it.
You've had today's move from me already. Patience. Tomorrow.
Again? No. One a day. Greed is the commonest blunder, {name}.

staff_caretaker.text: Morning. Entrance Hall's been swept twice already. Somebody always walks mud in by eight. Don't be somebody.
Up early, are we? Good. Trophies are next on my rounds. If you see a fingerprint on the glass, it wasn't me.
Morning rounds: the undercroft, the trophies, the gallery, the hall. Same as yesterday. Same as tomorrow. Suits me.
Afternoon. Courtyard's full of leaves, fountain's full of coins, and the clock court's full of students sitting where they shouldn't.
I'll be by the kitchens later, then the dungeons. Damp down there. Gets in the keys. Gets in the knees.
Locking up. Doors, windows, cupboards that think they're doors. Off to bed, before I lock you in by mistake.
It's late. The lamps stay lit all night by old promise, but that's no excuse for wandering. Go on. I didn't see you.
Every night I check every lock on the ground floor. Every night they're fine. One night they won't be. That's why I check.
Hear that? Forty-two keys. I know every one by its jingle. That one's the broom cupboard. That one's a mystery.
Mud. Always mud. From the grounds, the greenhouses, the paddock. Wipe your boots and you'll be my favourite. Briefly.
Quiet, please. Not for me. For the portraits. They get headaches. Then they complain to me.
Lost? Great Hall's that way, stairs are that way, and bed's up. You're all right.
Anything dropped in this castle comes to me in the end. Lost and found. Mostly found. Ask, if you're missing something.
The first lamp warden walked every floor twice a night and named every lamp. I don't name my keys. Well. A few.
The Trophy Stair gets polished by students on detention. Good for the stair, good for the students. Bad for my rags.
The courtyard portcullis hasn't come down in living memory. I still oil it. Habit. And the swallows like the smell.
Every spring I clean the courtyard fountain and put every single coin back. Don't ask why. Tradition. And bad luck not to.
That ladder up to the fortune-telling room has thirteen rungs. Students count twelve, or fourteen. Professors call it mystical. I call a carpenter.
Your house is top of the Cup. Doesn't mean you can walk mud through the hall. Winners wipe their boots too.
Behind in the Cup? Hand your work in and stop running in corridors. The points will come. That's my advice, free.
Tied at the top. Means a big feast and a big mess. Wonderful. More sweeping.
Dragonhide boots. Good soles. Very good soles. Wipe them anyway.
A cloak trailing on the floor picks up every speck of dust in the castle. You're sweeping my corridors for me. Thank you.
{house}, eh? Your lot leave the most mud. Loudest, too. Kind-hearted, mind. I'll give you that.
{house}. The only ones who ever offer to help me sweep. I always say no. I always appreciate it.
{house}. You leave books everywhere. Stairs, windowsills, the fountain once. I've a whole cupboard of them. Come and look.
{house}. Tidy, quiet, never in the wrong place at the wrong time. I'm watching you all the same.
Here's something for nothing: I saw a likely spot in {place} this morning. Worth a look, if you're quick about it.
Keep this under your hat. Have a poke about in {place} today. I'd do it myself, but my knees.
Found this on my rounds and nobody's claimed it, so it's yours now: {item}. Don't tell anyone I'm soft.
Lost property's overflowing. Take this off my hands: {item}. Go on.
Here. You've wiped your boots every time this week. I notice these things.
Already had something off me today. Don't push your luck. Tomorrow, maybe.
One a day, and you've had yours. Off you go. Mind the wet floor.

staff_librarian.text: Good morning. The first reader through the door always gets the best chair. Today, that could be you.
The morning shelving is the most peaceful part of my day. Let's keep it that way. Thank you.
At lunch I sit at the end of the staff table with a book propped on the teapot. The only quiet seat in the Great Hall.
The afternoon rush. Every desk taken, every candle lit. I love it. Quietly, of course.
If you're looking for something, ask. I know where everything is. Including the books people haven't returned.
We're closing soon. Please bring everything back to the desk, including the books hidden behind the cushions.
Lights out in the library. I trim every lamp myself. The shelves go to sleep one row at a time. My favourite part.
Let me see... all your books are returned. Oh, well done. You've no idea how happy that makes me.
A book returned late is a book someone else couldn't read. Please don't make me write you a polite little note. I will.
You've been reading! I can tell. There's a look. A faraway look, with a little ink on the nose.
If you have time, try the old castle histories. Dry as dust, but every so often a page surprises you.
The rule above our door asks for whispers. It was carved by a librarian with a booming voice. I admire her self-awareness.
The oldest inkwells refill themselves at midnight. Very convenient. Less so when a student leaves the lid off over a manuscript.
We keep every one of the stair architect's apologies. The last is two words long. It's the most borrowed item in the archive.
People come asking for the plans of the lost wing. They're in the archive. Please don't get your hopes up. The wing is very lost.
They say the painter of half our portraits painted herself forty times. I've checked the archive. It's at least forty-three.
Your house leads the Cup. Reading helps, you know. I'm only saying. Quietly.
Behind in the Cup? A good essay is worth a great many points, and I know where all the good books for essays are.
A tie at the top. Everyone's studying twice as hard. My library has never been so full. I'm in heaven. Shh.
A warm jumper. Good. The stacks are chilly, and readers who shiver turn pages too fast.
Dress robes. Very smart. Do keep the ink at a safe distance; the library cannot be held responsible for spills.
{house}. You read standing up, ready to rush off. Sit down. The book won't run away. Not the ones I keep, anyway.
{house}. You return everything on time, with a little thank-you. I keep the thank-yous in a drawer.
{house}. You've borrowed half my section on old charms. I'm thrilled. Bring them back all the same.
{house}. You always find the one book nobody has asked for in a century. How? Never mind. I'm impressed.
I've put something aside for you: a little piece of castle history, {lore}. Do read it slowly.
From the archive, for someone who'll appreciate it: {lore}. Please don't fold the corners.
A note someone left in a returned book mentions {place}. Something worth finding there today, I'd wager. Quietly, mind.
Between you and me, I'd have a look around {place} today. Readers notice things. So do librarians.
I've already given you something today. Tomorrow, perhaps. And do return what you borrowed.
That's enough for one day. Even the best readers must wait for the next chapter.

staff_groundskeeper.text: MORNING! Grand day for it! Whatever it is! I've fed the creatures, watered the beds and only fallen in the pond once.
Off to the greenhouses after this. The vines are lively this time of year. Lively means bitey. Wear gloves.
Morning rounds: paddock, greenhouses, courtyards. Then tea. Then the paddock again, because something's always got out.
Afternoon! Down to the lake, then the pitch, then up to the owls. These legs have walked the grounds more times than the path has.
I'll stop by the owls on the knoll before I lock the greenhouses. They like a chat. Well, I like a chat.
Getting dark soon. The lantern's lit over the paddock gate. Follow it if you're ever lost out here.
Don't mind the mud! Good honest mud, this. Tell the caretaker it was me. He knows. He always knows.
Talk kindly to the plants. I mean it. The ferns sulk if you don't, and a sulking fern is no use to anybody.
Bow at the paddock gate. Some creatures don't care, but the ones that do care a great deal. Costs nothing, saves your eyebrows.
That biting vine was bred to stop the mice. Works on mice. Works on gardeners too. Keep your sleeves rolled up. Trust me.
The shrieking roots get a rota so only one of us hears them at a time. My name's at the top again. Funny, that.
The greenhouses started with one pane of glass and one homesick lemon tree. Two hundred years later, look at 'em!
The paddock cats always sit facing the gate. Counting who comes in, so they know who to blame later. Clever beasts.
The potting shed clock runs on plant time. Slow in winter, quick in spring. I'm never on time for anything. I blame the clock.
The lantern over the paddock gate has never gone out. Every keeper trims it before bed. I'll trim it tonight. Always do.
Your house is top of the Cup! Ha! Like a prize marrow, that. Grew it yourselves, you did!
Behind in the Cup? Nothing grows overnight. Well, the glowcaps do. But nothing else. Keep watering!
All level at the top! Like the two prize pumpkins last autumn. We made 'em both into pies in the end. Everyone won.
Good thick jumper! You'll want that by the lake. The wind comes off the water like it's got somewhere to be.
Smart robes! Don't come near the vegetable beds in those. Or do. Mud's good for the soul.
Dragonhide boots! Those'll do for the paddock. Mind, the creatures can smell 'em. They'll want a word.
{house}! Brave enough to pet anything with teeth. Do ask first, though. Ask the creature, I mean. Then me.
{house}! Best hands in the greenhouses, your lot. Gentle with the seedlings, firm with the vines. Perfect.
{house}! You'll know the proper name of every plant out here. I just call 'em by how they bite. Works for me.
{house}! Patient lot. Good with the slow growers, and the ones that strike when you're not looking.
Here, the garden can spare this: {item}. Grew it myself. Well, it grew itself. I watched.
Take this, it's going spare: {item}. Good for brewing, the professors tell me. I mostly put it in soup.
Fresh from the beds: {item}. Still got the mud on. The mud's free.
You've had your share today! The garden needs a day to grow some more. Back tomorrow!
Nothing more today, friend. Even the best beds need a rest. Tomorrow!

shop_owl_exchange.text: Owl Exchange, good day! Fair prices, clean ledgers, no haggling. Well, a little haggling.
Ah, a customer! Buying, selling, browsing? Browsing's free. Everything else is very reasonable.
Welcome to the Exchange. Prices up to the minute. Well, up to the owl.
Good to see you, {name}. The ledger's open, the quills are sharpened, and so am I.
Morning! The first trade of the day is the luckiest. Let's make it a good one.
Afternoon rush, but there's always room at the counter for you. What can I do?
Late trading, eh? The owls are asleep, but the ledger never is. Go ahead.
Every trade written down, every coin accounted for. That's the Exchange's promise. Now, how can I help?
Socks, quills, feathers, fancies. If it's worth having, it's worth trading. Have a look.
Your house leads the Cup, I hear! Business always picks up for the winners. Celebrate with a purchase?
That's a fine outfit. Got the bits for it here? I've got the bits for most things.
Fair price, fair deal. Have a look, take your time, and do mind the inkpot.
The Exchange was founded to spare students the walk to the village. First trade on record: three quills for warm socks. Still the best deal in the ledger.
A clean ledger is a happy ledger. Mine has never had a blot. Well, one. It was a very cold morning.
Prices go up and prices go down. My advice? Buy when nobody wants it, sell when everybody does.
I've never short-changed a soul. I've short-changed myself twice, by accident. Both written down.

shop_owl_order_a.text: Catalogue's open! Everything's flying off the pages this week. Bold choices only, mind.
Hello, {name}! Fancy something new? I've just the thing. I always have just the thing.
Owl Order! Pick it, post it, wear it by Friday. Go on, be daring.
The velvet's selling fast this week. Fastest thing I've seen since the fireworks. Have a look.
Morning! The first owl's already been with today's catalogue. Hot off the press!
Afternoon! Half the common room's been in already. You're just in time.
Ordering at this hour? The owls fly at night anyway. Bold. I like it.
Your house leads the Cup! Treat yourself. Winners deserve a new hat.
Behind in the Cup? Nothing lifts the spirits like a bold new look. Trust me.
Oh, I love that jumper. There's a new knit in the catalogue that'd go a treat with it.
Something bold for the common room? A banner? A rug? Something that says 'here I am'?
What'll it be today? Don't think too long. That's not how this house shops.
Know what's selling fastest? Anything with a bit of nerve to it. Your lot never buy anything shy.
I've worked this stand for years. Never seen a common room that loves a bold colour more.
Order today and the owl will have it with you before you can change your mind. That's rather the point.

shop_owl_order_b.text: Hello, love. Take your time. There's no hurry here. There never is.
Catalogue's open. Sit by the fire while you look. No rush at all.
Something warm for the cold nights? We've just the thing. Several things, in fact.
Hello, {name}. Browse all you like. I'll be right here. I'm always right here.
Morning, love. Tea's brewing. Have a look while it steeps.
Afternoon. The quiet hour. Best time to pick something out properly.
Late, isn't it? Pick something cosy for bed. That's what the night's for.
Your house leads the Cup! Well deserved. Something to celebrate with?
All tied up at the top. Nervous? Cosy socks help. Truly.
That's a lovely knit. Look after it and it'll look after you. I've a few more like it.
We've some new rugs in. Soft as a sheepdog. Have a feel of the swatches.
Whatever you need, love. And if you don't need anything, that's fine too.
I never hurry anybody. Things chosen slowly are worn longest. That's my whole philosophy.
The best thing in the catalogue? A good warm pair of socks. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise.
I like this stand. Warm hearth, kind folk, and nobody ever shouts. Well, almost nobody.

shop_owl_order_c.text: Catalogue open. Every item measured, weighed and listed. Ask me anything about any of it.
Good day, {name}. The cloak on page four? Excellent weave. Very tight. I counted.
Welcome. I've annotated this week's catalogue. Only lightly. Forty pages.
Looking for something specific? I can tell you its thread count, its dye and its likely lifespan.
Morning. Clear head, clear choices. Shall we begin?
Good afternoon. I've reorganised the catalogue by fibre. It's far more sensible now.
Ordering by starlight? Very fitting. Do check the sizes twice. Starlight flatters.
Your house leads the Cup. Statistically unsurprising. Shall we mark the occasion?
Behind in the Cup. A temporary variance. Meanwhile, the felt hats are on page six.
A felt hat. Good choice. Felt holds its shape far better than people credit. I've done tests.
Every piece here is exactly what it says. I insist on it. Accuracy is a form of kindness.
Do take your time. Choosing well is a skill. Choosing quickly is merely a habit.
People ask why I care about thread counts. Because a thing made well is a thing that lasts. That's all.
I once sent back a whole order of scarves because the stripes were a millimetre off. The owl was very patient.
The catalogue has three printing errors this week. I've circled them. You're welcome.

shop_owl_order_d.text: Good evening. Or day. Whichever suits. The catalogue is open, and discreet.
Ah, {name}. I've marked a few pieces you might like. Understated. Excellent value. Nobody will guess.
Welcome. Everything here looks expensive. Not everything is. That's rather the point.
Looking for something with presence? Velvet, perhaps. It does the talking so you needn't.
Morning. A good choice made early saves a poor one made later.
Afternoon. The quiet hour. The best time for a considered purchase.
The late order. My favourite kind. Nobody sees what you chose until you wear it.
Your house leads the Cup. One should look the part. May I suggest page nine?
Behind in the Cup. Then look as though you aren't. Appearance is half of it.
Velvet. Impeccable. You already know what you're doing, so I'll merely hold the catalogue.
Quality needn't shout. Take your time. The best pieces are rarely on the front page.
I don't sell clothes. I sell impressions. The clothes come with them, naturally.
The trick, if you must know, is restraint. One fine thing, worn well, beats ten loud ones.
I've never told a customer something looks wonderful unless it did. That's why they believe me.
Some call the dungeons gloomy. I call it flattering light. Everyone looks mysterious down here.

students.text: Can't stop, late for class!
Have you done the essay? Me neither.
Morning! Is it morning? Feels like morning.
Oh, hello! See you in the common room later?
Hey, {house}! Good to see a friendly face.
Oi, {house}. No pinching our points, all right? Kidding. Mostly.
Hello! Don't tell my house I was nice to you.
Do you know where the Charms classroom is? I always forget.
The stairs moved on me again. Third time today.
I'm starving. Is it lunch yet?
Sorry, sorry, wasn't looking!
Lovely day for it. Whatever it is.
Shh, I'm revising. Sort of.
Have you seen my quill? Long, grey, slightly chewed?
I think a portrait just winked at me.
Potions next. Wish me luck.
If anyone asks, I was in the library.
Have you tried the treacle tart today? Go. Now.
Shouldn't we both be in bed?
Can't sleep. The castle creaks too much.
Nearly done for the day. Nearly.
Breakfast first, lessons second. That's the rule.
We're top of the Cup! Did you see the hourglass?
Your lot are top of the Cup this week. Enjoy it while it lasts!
We're behind in the Cup. Better earn some points, eh?
Everyone's level for the Cup. The common room's in uproar.
Nice jumper! Where'd you get it?
Dress robes on a weekday? Bold.
Your tie's crooked. There. Better.
The greenhouse vines bit me again.
Did you hear the kitchen bells ringing last night?
I'm off to the Dueling Club later. Want to come and watch me lose?
The owls are being very loud today.
Ugh, I've got ink all over my hands.
Hi! Sorry, can't chat, I'll be late.
Found anything good out on the grounds?
I swear this corridor was shorter yesterday.
Our ghost told me the same story again. I love it.
Don't run, the caretaker's about.
I'm off down to the lake. Want to come?
Still got two essays to write. Help.
Mind the puddle. The caretaker's furious about it.
